title: End of Year Teacher Clarity Booster: A Mission and a Project
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by reading the opening section of Cal Newport's Slow Productivity, Stuart argues that the final weeks of the school year are fertile ground for professional renewal rather than something to simply run out the clock on. His method is to zoom all the way out to the "Everest" purpose of his courses before zooming back in to something concrete: one last instructional project that reconnects him with that purpose. He offers several sample projects — additional rounds of MGCs with varied prompts, more pop-up debates on reflective end-of-year prompts, or a short student composition on the real-world usefulness of what they learned. The philosophizing, he argues, isn't indulgent; it "right-sizes" him, restoring the perspective that makes a small final project feel meaningful rather than an arbitrary add-on. He closes by distinguishing this from tacking a project onto students' plates — the point is the teacher's own reconnection with the fundamentals of the work, which happens to produce something with students as a byproduct.
points: Uses a two-step method (zoom out to course purpose, then zoom back in to one concrete project) as a repeatable technique for ending any teaching period with intention rather than exhaustion.
Explicitly credits Cal Newport's Slow Productivity as informing the piece, extending its "Do Fewer Things" principle into a classroom-specific application for the year's final weeks.
Offers a menu of concrete, low-prep project options — varied-prompt MGC rounds, reflective pop-up debates, a one-page usefulness composition — rather than a single prescribed activity.
Reframes the exercise as primarily about the teacher's own reconnection to purpose, with student benefit positioned as a secondary effect rather than the primary goal.
quotes: At the end of the school year, it's easy to get hypnotized by the bright light at the end of the tunnel, forgetting that these final weeks may prove the most fertile of soils for professional growth and regeneration.

My classes are meant to help my students grow into better thinkers, readers, writers, and speakers. These are the natural outcomes of doing things like writing essays, engaging in pop-up debates, analyzing sources, and building knowledge.

But how does such philosophizing help with ending the year strong? It restores my perspective; it right-sizes me. My work with students has immense weight in the grand scheme of things but is also very small in that grand scheme.
The point is you and me using our MISSION to create a simple, life-giving instructional PROJECT that we can complete between now and year's end.
I'm not talking about adding a student project to the end of your year; I'm talking about you and me setting out to do something that reconnects us with the fundamentals of our teaching.
